## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
and the bookmark derive from one bare title):

- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
  ready to be seen.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent, begun by a
sync that found `main` unmoved ([Sync](../AGENTS.md#sync)). Every
`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
   (`@` sits directly above it).
2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
   as it is.
3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
   cycle anymore.
5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
   disposal once fully merged.

- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.

**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

======
## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick the
case that fits your medium:

- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, ...).
    Add the case as needed
- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so `0.3.0-5.3.0`
    becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see [Unique per
  commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the per-commit
  preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If Rust,
  `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and leaves plain
  `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit flow's
  install.

**Single-name variant**: a repo striving to release makes the package name the binary's name, plain
`<name>` on `main` only:

- **The opening renames**: its bump sets `<name>-dev` beside the suffixed version, and every rung
  and the closing build under the dev name, the closing over the bare version.
- **Land restores**: the rename back to `<name>` is Land's act, so the stable name is only ever
  installed from what `main` will carry.
- **A build script guards the pairing** on every cargo verb: a suffixed version under the stable
  name fails the build, so no mid-cycle install can clobber the consumers' binary.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may bump
  less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in [Recording the
  version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA,
  which a commit cannot contain.

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
step without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its commits between
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the step),
so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference above, every
commit carries a distinct version.

# Bug list

Known defects we're aware of but haven't scheduled a fix for.
Each entry describes what goes wrong, when, and the cost of
the failure. Entries are numbered (`1.` `2.` ...) the same way
as `## Todo` in `TODO.md`. Run

## Bugs

1. **`push` `bookmark-set` races the git index lock.**
   `jj bookmark set` on the colocated work repo failed twice
   (the 0.69.0-3 and 0.69.0-4 pushes, same stage) with
   "Failed to reset Git HEAD state … could not acquire lock
   for `.git/index` … after 1 attempt(s)". The lockfile was
   already gone on inspection seconds later. Seen again at
   the 0.75.0-2 push (which also triggered #3) and the
   0.77.0-0 push (2026-07-28), four occurrences, always at
   `bookmark-set`, always transient.
   - **Cost:** push aborts mid-flow (rollback restored both
     repos cleanly both times), and recovery is a `--restart`
     rerun, which succeeded both times.
   - The bot thinks a git-aware watcher (shell prompt,
     editor) briefly re-reads the repo after the commit
     stages touch `.git`, holding the index lock exactly
     when `bookmark-set` resets git HEAD, and jj gives up
     after a single attempt.
   - **Fix direction** (two options, possibly combined):
     - retry with short backoff around the bookmark-set
41:   - **Fixed at 0.78.0-8**, both options combined as

384:    - **Fixed** by "fix: clone says the right dir and stops on a rejected config".
399:    - **Fixed** by "fix: clone says the right dir and stops on a rejected config": both cases

## In Progress

### fix: no test sets HOME

(wink + agent, 2026-10-15) `init::tests::expand_vars_tilde` sets `HOME` to `/h` for the whole
test process and puts it back, and a test that signs a commit while it is set has git look for
the signing key under `/h`, so `vc-x1 validate` fails now and then for no reason in the change
under it. [Bug 21](notes/bugs.md#bugs), seen a second time 2026-10-15, its victim
`init::tests::dual_fixture_writes_work_and_bot_config_files`.

#### Deliberation

- Fixed now, ahead of the Todo's first entry, wink's call: a validation that fails at random
  stops every cycle's push.
- The fix is the bug's own fix direction: `expand_vars` reads `HOME` and hands it to an inner
  function that takes the home directory as an argument, and the test calls the inner one.
  - Running the tests single-threaded, as the test's comment suggests, was not taken: it slows
    every run to hide one test's write.
- Single-step, one function split and its record.

#### Solution

`expand_vars` splits so the expansion takes the home directory as an argument, and the test of
`~` passes `/h` instead of writing `HOME`, so no test writes the process's `HOME`.

#### Acceptance check

- `rg 'set_var\("HOME"' src/` prints nothing.
- `vc-x1 validate` passes.

#### Ladder

- fix: no test sets HOME (current)

content.text:
No, I didn't reproduce it.

- **What I ran:** one more `cargo test` before the fix, and the full `vc-x1 validate` after it. Both passed, but a pass doesn't tell us much when the failure is rare. Bug 21 records about one failure in a dozen runs.
- **Why I think this is the cause:** the error says it looked for the key at `/h/.ssh/git-commits-wink@saville.com.pub`. The only place `/h` comes from is `expand_vars_tilde` setting `HOME` to `/h`. The test that failed signs a commit, and git expands `~` in the signing-key path using `HOME`. The first sighting, on 2026-10-11, had the same message with a different victim test.
- **What that doesn't prove:** that the race actually happens the way I described, or that the fix closes it. Right now the fix stands on reasoning plus a search showing nothing else in `src/` sets `HOME`.

A deterministic reproduction is possible, and it wouldn't touch the repos:
1. Export `main` into the session's scratchpad.
2. Add a sleep to the old `expand_vars_tilde` while `HOME` is `/h`, so the window is seconds wide instead of microseconds.
3. Run it alongside the fixture test, and it should fail with the same message.
4. Apply the same change to the fixed code, and it should pass, because nothing writes `HOME` there.

The cost is a fresh build in the scratchpad, probably a few minutes. Should I run it before you continue the review?

# Process-spawn ban, since 0.79.0. The mechanism, the ban as config,
# the grant as an attribute, this comment as the register, is
# explained in README.md under "No process spawns". A new
# `Command::new` site needs an entry below and a visible
# `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` naming it.
#
# The register, closed (wink, 2026-08-19), reopened for entries 5
# and 6:
#
# 1. Version gate: the `jj -V` probe (src/version.rs). The gate
#    exists to compare the user's jj CLI against our jj-lib, so the
#    CLI spawn is its subject matter.
# 2. Push's `$EDITOR` launch (src/push.rs): interactive message
#    editing is a spawn by definition.
# 3. Init's gh provisioning (src/init.rs): `gh auth status`,
#    `gh repo view`, `gh repo create`. Creating a repo on GitHub is
#    the forge's REST API, not a version-control operation, and no jj or
#    git library can do it, and gh is GitHub's authenticated client.
# 4. Test helpers (src/test_helpers.rs and tests/common/mod.rs):
#    real-jj/git fixture setup and interop verification, kept
#    deliberately independent of the facade under test, and never a
#    substitute for asserting our jj-lib paths directly. The CLI
#    tests' launcher spawning the built vc-x1 binary is this entry
#    too: spawning the binary is what a CLI test is.
# 5. The validate subcommand (src/validate.rs): runs the
#    workspace's configured `[validate]` commands, which is its
#    whole job. Opened 2026-08-21 by the "empty custom-family into
#    the pinned set and config" cycle, whose plan put the checklist
#    commands in config for one subcommand to run.
# 6. Sync's remote look (src/jj/session.rs, `git_command`): two
#    git commands that ask a remote and move no ref. `git ls-remote
#    --heads <remote>` gives the commit each of the remote's
#    bookmarks is on, and `git fetch --refmap= --no-tags
#    --no-write-fetch-head` downloads the commits of the ones that
#    moved, so a fast-forward can be told from a rewrite before
#    anything is fetched. Sync has to know what a fetch would do
#    before it makes one, and a fetch changes the repo. jj-lib has no
#    such query: it spawns git itself for its network legs and keeps
#    that layer private, and it builds gix with no network client,
#    as of 0.45.1 and 0.46.0. Opened 2026-10-09 (wink) by the
#    "feat: sync is safe by default" cycle, and temporary: the entry
#    closes when jj-lib offers the query (TODO.md > ## Waiting).

content.text:
Not as a test that reproduces the race. After the fix there's no `HOME` write left to race against, so a reproduction would always pass and prove nothing. What a test can do is either show the mechanism or stop the cause from coming back.

1. **Mechanism test** (I'd skip this): run the built `vc-x1 init` as a child process with `HOME=/h` in that child's environment only, so nothing races, and with commit signing turned on. Then assert that the commit fails with "Couldn't load public key /h/...".
   - It's deterministic, but what it tests is git's behaviour, which we don't own.
   - It needs `ssh-keygen` and a signing key, which some machines won't have.
   - It doesn't guard our own code against anything.
2. **Recurrence guard** (recommended): make the cause fail `vc-x1 validate`, using the same mechanism as the process-spawn ban in `clippy.toml`.
   - Add `std::env::set_var` and `std::env::remove_var` to `disallowed-methods`, with a reason that cites bug 21.
   - The two sites that remain get a visible `#[allow]` each:
     - `expand_vars_envvar` in `src/init/tests.rs`, which uses its own variable.
     - `tests/cli_keep.rs`, which is its own test binary and already explains why its write is safe.
   - From then on, a new environment write anywhere fails clippy until someone justifies it at the site.

Option 2 enforces exactly what this cycle's title says, so it can go in this same commit. Nothing has been pushed apart from the bookmark, and the cycle stays single-step. I'd add one line to the acceptance check, "clippy rejects a new `set_var`", which I'd confirm by adding a call temporarily and watching `vc-x1 validate --fast` fail.

Should I add option 2 to this commit, file it as a Todo instead, or both?

The plain version: we can't write a test that recreates the failure, because the fix removed what caused it. We can make the linter refuse anything that would bring that cause back.

content.text:
Ah, you mean a test that fails on the code before the fix and passes after it. That's possible, with one limit.

**The limit:** the failure itself can't be reproduced reliably. It's a timing race: the signing test has to make its commit in the microseconds while `HOME` is `/h`. To force that timing, a test would have to write `HOME` itself, which is what we're removing, or add a pause hook to the old test, so it would no longer be testing the code as it was.

**What can fail reliably before the fix is the cause.** The test would be `no_test_writes_home`:
- It walks `src/` and `tests/` under `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`.
- It fails on any `set_var("HOME"` or `remove_var("HOME"`, naming the file and line.
- On the old code it fails every time and points at `src/init/tests.rs:549`. With the fix it passes.

**How I'd show red, then green, without losing the fix:**
1. Add the test.
2. Move the fixed `src/init/tests.rs` into `tmp/`, put `main`'s version back, and run the new test. It should fail and point at line 549.
3. Restore the fixed file and run it again. It should pass.
4. Then run the full `vc-x1 validate`.

**Its weakness:** it matches text, so `set_var(key, ...)` with `key` holding `"HOME"` would slip past. The clippy ban I mentioned earlier doesn't have that gap, but it fails at lint time rather than as a test. The two can go together.

This stays inside the cycle's subject, and nothing has been pushed but the bookmark, so it can go in this same commit. It would add one line to the acceptance check: `no_test_writes_home` failed before the fix and passes after it.

Should I go ahead with the test alone, or with the test plus the clippy ban?

The plain version: we can't reliably recreate the bad timing, but we can write a test that catches the cause. It fails on the old code and passes on the new.

content.text:
Yes, it would work, with two caveats.

**Where the sleep goes:** it has to sit inside the window, between the old test's `set_var("HOME", "/h")` and its restore.
- Inside the old `expand_vars_tilde` itself is best.
- Putting it in `expand_vars` would also make every init fixture sleep, since init calls `expand_vars` for its paths.
- I'd gate it with `#[cfg(test)]` rather than `debug_assertions`. `cfg(test)` means test builds only, while `debug_assertions` would also slow `cargo run` and every debug build.

**The caveats:**
1. **It makes the failure likely, not certain.** A three-second sleep widens the window, but a signing test still has to happen to run during it. With 653 tests spread across threads, that will almost always happen. It also only fails where commits are signed, as they are on your machine. On a machine without signing configured it stays green.
2. **It stops mattering once the fix is in.** The fixed test never writes `HOME`, so there's no window left to widen. The sleep would protect against nothing and would only add three seconds to every run. So it's a demonstration, not a lasting test.

**My suggestion is to use it for exactly that:**
1. **Red:** put `main`'s `src/init/tests.rs` back, add a three-second sleep inside the window, and run `cargo test`. I'd expect one or more signing tests to fail with "Couldn't load public key /h/...". That confirms the cause we've been assuming.
2. **Green:** restore the fixed file, which has no sleep and nothing to sleep in, and run `cargo test` again. Everything should pass.
3. Nothing from steps 1 and 2 gets committed. I'd note the result in the cycle's deliberation.
4. Commit the lasting guard: the `no_test_writes_home` test, the clippy ban, or both, whichever you pick.

Should I run the red/green demonstration now? And for the lasting guard, do you want the test, the clippy ban, or both?

The plain version: yes, a deliberate pause would make the failure show up almost every time on the old code, which proves the cause. Once the fix is in, the pause has nothing to protect against, so we'd use it once and then keep a cheaper guard.

content.content:
## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

([why](rationale.md#-ok--comments-on-unwrap-calls-rust))

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a lean,
not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a silently
  substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are not
    used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and appropriate
  uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site when the crate enables the
  project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`, the recommended base:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit flow)

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

([why](rationale.md#-ok--comments-on-unwrap-calls-rust))

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a lean,
not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a silently
  substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.

    register's two entries.

content.text:
Because the environment belongs to the whole process, and our tests run as threads inside one process. The ban makes every write to it a choice someone has to justify.

1. **Every write is visible to every other test.** `cargo test` runs a test binary's tests as threads of one process, and that process has one environment. A test that changes a variable changes it for every test running at the same moment, and for every child process those tests spawn. That is bug 21, and the demonstration showed it twice:
   - git looked for your signing key under `/h`;
   - the `jj` children of the sync tests found no config.
2. **A write can race even when no other test reads that variable.** libc's `setenv` and `getenv` aren't thread-safe. A write in one thread while another thread reads any variable, including git, jj-lib, or a spawn copying the environment, is undefined behaviour and can crash. That's why Rust 2024 made `set_var` and `remove_var` `unsafe`.

**Why ban both calls outright, rather than just `HOME`?**
- Point 2 applies to any variable, and point 1 applies to any variable some other code reads. `tests/cli_keep.rs` is a separate test binary for exactly that reason: `VC_X1_TEST_KEEP` is read by every fixture's `Drop`.
- A name-specific check also misses a variable that holds the name. That is the gap in `no_test_writes_home`.
- Banning the calls makes every site visible: the `#[allow]` sits in the diff, and the register in `clippy.toml` says why that site is safe. It's the same pattern this project already uses for `Command::new`.
- It costs nothing in the program itself: vc-x1's non-test code has no environment writes. If it ever needs to give a child process a variable, `Command::env` sets it for the child alone.

**One caveat about what the register grants:** entry 1, `expand_vars_envvar`, is safe from point 1 because no other test reads its variable, but not from point 2, since it still writes while other tests' threads read. It could go the way `HOME` did: `expand_vars_with_home` would also take the variable lookup as an argument, and the test would pass a closure instead of setting anything. That would leave entry 2, the single-test binary, as the only write anywhere. It's about 15 more lines. Should I add it to this commit, or leave the register at two entries?

The plain version: environment variables are shared by every test running at once, and changing one can break or even crash an unrelated test. So the linter now refuses any change to them unless the site says why it's safe.

content.content:
### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
  form, the general form at its smallest.
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are

### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.

  form, the general form at its smallest.

  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

## In Progress

### fix: no test sets HOME

(wink + agent, 2026-10-15) `init::tests::expand_vars_tilde` sets `HOME` to `/h` for the whole
test process and puts it back, and a test that signs a commit while it is set has git look for
the signing key under `/h`, so `vc-x1 validate` fails now and then for no reason in the change
under it. [Bug 21](notes/bugs.md#bugs), seen a second time 2026-10-15, its victim
`init::tests::dual_fixture_writes_work_and_bot_config_files`.

#### Deliberation

- Fixed now, ahead of the Todo's first entry, wink's call: a validation that fails at random
  stops every cycle's push.
- The fix is the bug's own fix direction: `expand_vars` reads `HOME` and hands it to an inner
  function that takes the home directory as an argument, and the test calls the inner one.
  - Running the tests single-threaded, as the test's comment suggests, was not taken: it slows
    every run to hide one test's write.
- The cause was reproduced before the fix was trusted, wink's ask at review: the failure itself
  was not, a race seen once in about a dozen runs.
  - A three-second sleep inside the old test's window, `main`'s test file under the fixed
    code, failed 18 sync integration tests: the `jj` they spawn inherited `HOME=/h`, found no
    config, and died with "Failed to determine the secure config for a repo". A different
    symptom from the signing key, the same cause.
  - The fixed test with the same sleep: all 653 passed.
  - The sleep was a demonstration and is not committed: after the fix there is no window for it
    to widen.
- Two guards keep the cause out, wink's call at review, both:
  - The test `no_test_writes_home` scans `src/` and `tests/` for a write of `HOME`, so it fails
    on `main`'s test file, naming its three writes, and passes on the fix. It matches text, so
    a variable holding `"HOME"` passes it.
  - Clippy bans `std::env::set_var` and `std::env::remove_var`, as it bans `Command::new`, with
    a register in `clippy.toml` and an `#[allow]` at each granted site. That covers the variable
    the test misses. The two remaining writes, each of a variable no other test reads, are the
    register's two entries.
  - Entry 1, `expand_vars_envvar`, still writes while other tests' threads read the
    environment, which libc does not make safe. Passing it a variable lookup, as `HOME` is
    passed, would retire it, and it stays, wink's call: the register leaves it visible.
- Single-step, one function split, its guards, and its record.

#### Solution

`expand_vars` splits so the expansion takes the home directory as an argument, and the test of
`~` passes `/h` instead of writing `HOME`, so no test writes the process's `HOME`. A test fails
on any write of `HOME`, and clippy bans environment writes but for the two sites its register
names.

- `cargo clippy --all-targets` rejects an environment write without an `#[allow]`: the ban
  flagged the four writes in `src/init/tests.rs` and `tests/cli_keep.rs` before their `#[allow]`s.
- `vc-x1 validate` passes.

### A validation failure is investigated before it is run again

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) A full validation failed once in the closing of the cycle **docs: the
session lock is settled as flock**, with no code changed, and the agent ran it again, saw it
pass, and reported that. A pass on the second run says nothing of why the first failed, and wink
wants the failure looked into first.

- The failure: `init::tests::adopt_keeps_a_gitignore_that_has_the_line` and
  `fix_desc::tests::por_workspace_noops` each died making a commit, on "Couldn't load public key
  /h/.ssh/git-commits-wink@saville.com.pub". The runs before and after passed all 650.
- The cause, we think: a test in `src/init/tests.rs` sets `HOME` to `/h` for the whole test
  process while it checks `expand_vars`, and puts it back. A test running beside it that signs
  a commit in that moment looks for the signing key under `/h`.
  - The fix is that test taking its home as an argument, or the tests that read `HOME` running

So I kept the entry, as the cycle's title says ("keeps only its rule"). It closes when an `agent-files` proposal cycle adds the rule to the Validate step.

content.text:
You probably mean the per-rung flow. It's the section of `AGENTS.md` titled [The per-rung flow](AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow). A "rung" is one commit of a cycle: the opening, each step in between, or the closing. For a single-step cycle, it's the cycle's one commit.

The per-rung flow is the nine steps every such commit goes through, and the agent reads them from the file right before doing them:

1. **Mark current:** mark the rung `(current)` in the In Progress block.
2. **Bump:** bump the version to this commit's version.
3. **Work:** do the work, and stop and ask on any deviation from the plan.
4. **Rung subsection:** record what the rung changed, conceptually.
5. **Validate:** run `vc-x1 validate` before every review.
6. **Work review:** say "please review" and wait for "continue" or "go".
7. **Flip and describe:** flip `(current)` to `(done)`, then write the commit description.
8. **Description review:** show the title and body, and ask permission to push.
9. **Commit + push:** `vc-x1 push`, then stop.

The Todo's rule would add to step 5. Right now step 5 only says to run validation. The proposal is that when a run fails, the agent reads the failure and names its cause before running it again, and that a failure which doesn't repeat counts as a finding, reported and given a Todo entry. That's the agent-file change the next cycle would make.

Yes, that's cleaner. The entry stops being a Todo and becomes the plan for the next cycle. Two details to settle first:

**1. Where "the next change" is written.** I'd use the continuation notes in `zDOING.md`, which are for exactly this: what the next agent acts on first. The note would say that the next cycle is an `agent-files` proposal adding the rule to step 5 (Validate) of the per-rung flow, and would carry the rule's text, so nothing from the entry is lost. That agent's acquaint reads the note, opens that cycle with the rule as its subject, and resets the note.

**2. Changing the pushed chore.** The commit's current title, "...keeps only its rule", would be wrong once the entry is gone. Since the bookmark hasn't landed yet:
- The content is amended in place: the entry is removed from `TODO.md`, the note is added, and the chore's record in `zCLOSED.md` is updated.
- The title and body get a coordinated re-describe that keeps the `ochid:` trailer. Rewording an already-pushed commit needs your go, so this message is asking for it. The new title would be `chore: the validation-failure Todo retires to the per-rung flow change`.
- Then the bookmark is force-pushed, which is a push and needs your approval.

The alternative is to land the chore as it is and let the proposal cycle's opening move the entry out of `## Todo`. That retires it one cycle later, and nothing gets rewritten.

## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer

**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
coordinating with everyone involved first**
([why](rationale.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer)). It is a history rewrite,
and it silently drops the cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been
described and carries no trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not
covered. That is a [local
ladder](../AGENTS.md#local-ladders)'s scratch describe.

When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one already
stamped). Hit at a coordinated amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that way.
`vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.

content.content:
## Advancing X.Y.Z: patch by default

Which of the three numbers moves is not a classification problem
([why](rationale.md#advancing-xyz-patch-by-default)): **patch by default, minor by the user's call,
major by the project's promise.**

- **Patch by default**: every cycle advances `Z`, whatever it touched. Code or docs, large or small,
  none of it matters, so the choice costs no deliberation.
- **Minor is deliberate and rare**: the user names it at a cycle's opening when the change deserves
  a visible marker in the history, and the agent never infers it from a change's content or size.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its users.
  A project that makes that promise records it as its local edit of this rule, and absent one the
  default above governs.

## Agent-files version

The agent-files set has a version of its own, apart from the artifact's, so which set an adopter
carries is read from a listing rather than a diff, and an `agent-files` title has a token that is
unique by construction ([Project-declared types](prose.md#project-declared-types),
[why](rationale.md#agent-files-version)).

- **Record**: an empty file, `agent-data/agent-files-vX.Y.Z{-suffix}`, the version its name. `ls
  agent-data` shows it without a read, a bump is a rename, and
  `git log --diff-filter=A -- 'agent-data/agent-files-v*'` lists every version beside the commit
  that introduced it.
- **Spelling**: `vX.Y.Z` everywhere the agent-files version is written, the file name, an
  `agent-files` title, and vc-x1's output, so `agent-files v0.1.0` reads the same in all three. The
  `v` is the name-plus-version pair as cargo prints it (`bar v1.0.0`), and a tool's own banner stays
  bare (`vc-x1 0.82.0`), so a `v` number is the set's and a bare one the artifact's.
- **Proposals bump, adoptions copy**: a proposal cycle bumps it at the opening, advancing per
  [Advancing X.Y.Z](#advancing-xyz-patch-by-default), and its rungs walk the [Suffix
  scheme](#suffix-scheme) beside the artifact's version, `-0`, `-1`, then bare at the close-out, so
  a set copied from a draft bookmark says on its face that it is unfinished. An adoption copies the
  source's bare file and bumps nothing.
- **An adoption is a copy and a check**: `vc-x1 agent-files copy -c <src>` takes the set and the
  family's `custom.md` with it, and `vc-x1 agent-files diff -c <src>` is the adoption's last act,
  exiting zero when the two copies are the same. An adopter that keeps a `custom.md` of its own
  drops the `-c` from both, which is its prerogative.
- **Agreed**: the payload's number is the family's agreed version. An adopter ahead of it is
  proposing, one behind has not re-synced, and two proposers claiming one number are settled by the
  maintainer at convergence, the loser re-proposing under the next.
- **Which digit**: tend toward the patch digit, kept to one digit and rolled over into the minor.
  We think the minor stays within two digits and major increments when the family decides.

  `v` is the name-plus-version pair as cargo prints it (`bar v1.0.0`), and a tool's own banner stays
  bare (`vc-x1 0.82.0`), so a `v` number is the set's and a bare one the artifact's.
- **Proposals bump, adoptions copy**: a proposal cycle bumps it at the opening, advancing per
  [Advancing X.Y.Z](#advancing-xyz-patch-by-default), and its rungs walk the [Suffix
  scheme](#suffix-scheme) beside the artifact's version, `-0`, `-1`, then bare at the close-out, so
  a set copied from a draft bookmark says on its face that it is unfinished. An adoption copies the
  source's bare file and bumps nothing.
- **An adoption is a copy and a check**: `vc-x1 agent-files copy -c <src>` takes the set and the
  family's `custom.md` with it, and `vc-x1 agent-files diff -c <src>` is the adoption's last act,
  exiting zero when the two copies are the same. An adopter that keeps a `custom.md` of its own
  drops the `-c` from both, which is its prerogative.
- **Agreed**: the payload's number is the family's agreed version. An adopter ahead of it is
  proposing, one behind has not re-synced, and two proposers claiming one number are settled by the
  maintainer at convergence, the loser re-proposing under the next.
- **Which digit**: tend toward the patch digit, kept to one digit and rolled over into the minor.
  We think the minor stays within two digits and major increments when the family decides.
